Dear Daniel,
First, many thanks for your package: survey facilities are a very useful feature!!
I am currently trying to use it for an application with propensity score matching.

design.ps <http://design.ps> <- svydesign(ids = ~1, weights = ~w, data = ImputedListWithWeights)
I found this line of code in McCaffrey 2004, "Propensity score estimation with boosted regression for evaluating causal effects in observational studies"

liss.implist <- lapply(seq(liss.imp$m), function(im) complete(liss.imp, im))

library("mitools")

I find that the resulting object is not as easy to manipulate so I would rather skip this bit if not necessary.
Best Regards and thanks a lot again!
JB

messages.body_plain:
On 05/31/2014 10:15 PM, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> The Bollen-Stine (or "model-based") bootstrap rescales the observed data
> so that they are consistent with the null hypothesis of perfect fit
> (i.e., it begins by transforming the data so that the observed means and
> covariance matrix are identical to the model-implied means and
> covariance matrix).  This is so that the bootstrapped distribution of
> chi-squared statistics (and by implication, the p-value/probability of a
> chi-sq at least as large as your observed chi-sq) is consistent with the
> null hypothesis.  You do not use Bollen-Stine method to calculate SEs or
> CIs for your parameters.

Note that if you specify se="bootstrap", and test="bollen-stine", then
'bollen-stine' is used for both SEs and the test statistic. But for the
SEs, this has (almost) no impact.

Yves.

messages.subject_clean: Phantom Variables and Bentler & Raykov (2000) Rsq
messages.body_plain:
First, my apologies: the " =~ 0 " trick is NOT broken in 0.5-16. It only
breaks if you do

lavaanify(' f =~ 0 ')

without anything else.

Anyway, I had a look at the Raykov & Bentler (2000) paper. To define 'V1
- E1', we must define E1 as a phantom variable too. This is not
necessary in the Bentler-Weeks world, but it is in the
LISREL/lavaan/Mplus world.

For reference, below is the lavaan syntax reproducing the results from
Appendix B.

Yves.

library(lavaan)

# Raykov and Bentler (2000) - Figure 1
lower <- '
     1.0
     0.75   1.0
     0.25   0.1   1.0
     0.1875 0.375 0.0 1.0 '
COV <- getCov(lower, names=c("V1","V2","V3","V4"))

model <- '
     E1 =~ 0; E1 ~~ E1
     E2 =~ 0; E2 ~~ E2
     V1 ~~ 0*V1; V2 ~~ 0*V2
     V1 ~ V2 + V3 + 1*E1
     V2 ~ V1 + V4 + 1*E2

     F1 =~ 0
     F2 =~ 0

     F1 ~ 1*V1 + (-1)*E1
     F2 ~ 1*V2 + (-1)*E2
'

fit <- sem(model, sample.cov=COV, sample.nobs=200, mimic="EQS")
summary(fit)

# use inspect to extract correlations
COR.ALL <- inspect(fit, "cor.all")
R2.V1 <- COR.ALL["F1","V1"]^2
R2.V1
R2.V2 <- COR.ALL["F2","V2"]^2
R2.V2

# Raykov and Bentler (2000) - Figure 2
lower <- ' 1.0
            0.6163 1.0
            0.5    0.2 1.0
            0.0    0.3 0.0 1.0 '
COV <- getCov(lower, names=c("V1","V2","V3","V4"))

model <- '
     E1 =~ 0; E1 ~~ E1
     E2 =~ 0; E2 ~~ E2
     V1 ~~ 0*V1; V2 ~~ 0*V2

     V1 ~ V3 + 1*E1
     V2 ~ V1 + V4 + 1*E2
     E1 ~~ E2

     F1 =~ 0
     F2 =~ 0

     F1 ~ 1*V1 + (-1)*E1
     F2 ~ 1*V2 + (-1)*E2
'

fit <- sem(model, sample.cov=COV, sample.nobs=200, mimic="EQS")
summary(fit)

# use inspect to extract correlations
COR.ALL <- inspect(fit, "cor.all")
R2.V1 <- COR.ALL["F1","V1"]^2
R2.V1
R2.V2 <- COR.ALL["F2","V2"]^2
R2.V2

>

In fact, you can do this using the cfa() function. You can 'override'
the fix-first-loading-to-one default by using the 'NA*' modifier. And
you also need to 'label' the first indicator. Since you can only use one
modifier at a time, you must repeat the first indicator on the right
hand side, each time with a different indicator:

HS.model <- '

     textual =~ NA*x4 + t1*x4 + t2*x5 + t3*x6

     v1 == 3 - v2 - v3
     t1 == 3 - t2 - t3
     s1 == 3 - s2 - s3
'

fit <- cfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939)
summary(fit)

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I've been testing the measurement invariance between a group of people with and without a chronic disease on a latent well-being scale (5 continuous indicators). I used the lavaan.survey package as I also have to apply sample weights. Now I want to test if the two groups score significantly different on the mean of the latent variable. First I want to test this without other control variables, in a second step I also want to include other controlling variables (so compare the means after checking for the influence of other variables on the latent well-being variable). (Asyou will notice, I am a new user to lavaan and lavaan.survey, so please correct me if I'm wrong)

How should I include the controls?

==> My current syntax:

#specify model
who5 <-'who_5wellbeing =~ Y11_Q45a2 + Y11_Q45b2 + Y11_Q45c2 + Y11_Q45d2 + Y11_Q45e2'

#apply weights
survey.design<-svydesign(ids=~1, data=newdata_belgium, weights=~weights)

#step1: configural invariance - estimation
config_fit3 <- cfa(who5, data=newdata_belgium, estimator="MLR", group="chronic")
survey.config_fit3<-lavaan.survey(lavaan.fit=config_fit3, survey.design=survey.design)

summary(survey.config_fit3, standardized=TRUE, fit.measures=TRUE)
?modindices
subset(modindices(survey.config_fit), mi>5)

#step2: weak invariance - estimation

weak_fit3 <- cfa(who5, data=newdata_belgium, estimator="MLR", group="chronic", group.equal="loadings")
survey.weak_fit3<-lavaan.survey(lavaan.fit=weak_fit3, survey.design=survey.design)

summary(survey.weak_fit3, standardized=TRUE, fit.measures=TRUE)

#step3: strong invariance - estimation

strong_fit3 <- cfa(who5, data=newdata_belgium, estimator="MLR", group="chronic", group.equal=c("loadings", "intercepts"))
survey.strong_fit3<-lavaan.survey(lavaan.fit=strong_fit3, survey.design=survey.design)

summary(survey.strong_fit3, standardized=TRUE, fit.measures=TRUE)

subset(modindices(survey.strong_fit3), mi>5)

#comparing nested models
anova (survey.config_fit3, survey.weak_fit3) #weak invariance yes
anova(survey.weak_fit3, survey.strong_fit3)  #strong invariance no, partial invariance?

#step3.1: partial strong invariance - estimation

partial_fit3 <- cfa(who5, data=newdata_belgium, estimator="MLR", group="chronic", group.equal=c("loadings", "intercepts"), group.partial=c("Y11_Q45c2~1"))
survey.partial_fit3<-lavaan.survey(lavaan.fit=partial_fit3, survey.design=survey.design)

#comparing nested models
anova(survey.weak_fit3, survey.partial_fit3) #yes, partial invariance

messages.body_plain:
> ==> After these steps I want to compare the means of the groups as well: is the following step correct?

>
> anova(means_fit4, survey.partial_fit3)

Assuming you are interpreting your output correctly, yes, the logic of the above steps seems sound.  But your call to anova() to test the latent means should take the survey weights into account first:   anova(survey.means_fit4, survey.partial_fit3)

>
> ==> After this step I want to compare the means of the groups, but also check for the relation between other control variables and the laten variable: how do I proceed? ... is there a different/better option?

This is a bit more nuanced.  The additional regressions in your new model "who5_controls" are correct, but to test whether means can be constrained to equality after controlling for age, gender, education, and SES, you need to run that model with and without constraining the latent means, then call anova() to compare the two.  However, if you allow the regression slopes for the control variables to differ between groups, that is equivalent to estimating an interaction term between "chronic" and each control variable.  If you were to code "chronic" as a dummy variable (assuming 2 groups only for simplicity), the regression model would look something like this:

> wellbeing ~ (intercept) + chronic + age + gender + education + SES + chronic:age + chronic:gender + chronic:education + chronic:SES

So constraining the latent "means" (actually constraining latent intercepts because the latent variable has predictors) would only test whether the means were equivalent when age, gender, education, and SES all == 0.  I don't think this is a meaningful comparison/test, because you would be forcing the effect of "chronic" to be zero, but still estimating its interactions with controls.

> wellbeing ~ (intercept) + 0*chronic + age + gender + education + SES + chronic:age + chronic:gender + chronic:education + chronic:SES

If you want to test the latent mean-differences while controlling for age, gender, education, and SES, you need to constrain the effects of the control variables across "chronic" groups as well (i.e., get rid of the interaction terms).  The first thing I would do is (1) include control variables (unconstrained across groups) in the model where means are also unconstrained.  Then (2) test whether you can constrain the effects of control variables (i.e., get rid of the interactions between "chronic" and each control).  If that is tenable, then the mean-difference between "chronic" groups does not depend on any of the control variables, so (3) you can run another model with mean constrained to see if that is tenable.

who5_controls <- '
#latent variable
who_5wellbeing =~ Y11_Q45a2 + Y11_Q45b2 + Y11_Q45c2 + Y11_Q45d2 + Y11_Q45e2
#regression

who_5wellbeing ~ education + labourmarketposition + age + gender
'
## (1)
controls_fit5 <- cfa(who5_controls, data = newdata_belgium,
                     estimator = "MLR", group = "chronic",
                     group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts"),
                     group.partial = c("Y11_Q45c2~1"))
survey.controls_fit5 <- lavaan.survey(lavaan.fit = controls_fit5, survey.design = survey.design)

## (2)
controls_fit6 <- cfa(who5_controls, data = newdata_belgium,
                     estimator = "MLR", group = "chronic",
                     group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts", "regressions"),
                     group.partial = c("Y11_Q45c2~1"))
survey.controls_fit6 <- lavaan.survey(lavaan.fit = controls_fit6, survey.design = survey.design)

## Test whether effects of controls are similar across "chronic" groups

anova(survey.controls_fit5, survey.controls_fit6)

## If this is tenable, you can test an "overall" mean-difference across "chronic" groups

## (3)

controls_fit7 <- cfa(who5_controls, data = newdata_belgium,
                     estimator = "MLR", group = "chronic",
                     group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts", "regressions", "means"),
                     group.partial = c("Y11_Q45c2~1"))
survey.controls_fit7 <- lavaan.survey(lavaan.fit = controls_fit7, survey.design = survey.design)

## Test whether effects of controls are similar across "chronic" groups

anova(survey.controls_fit6, survey.controls_fit7)

You may need to run more models after (2) to see which (if any) regressions cannot be constrained across groups.  But if even one of them can't be, then the effect of that control variable differs across groups, so you could only test the effect of "chronic" at particular levels of the control(s).  If you can pick certain levels (e.g., particular ages, or both sexes) where that would be a meaningful test, then you can recode your data and re-run models to test the mean-difference at those levels.

Terry

messages.subject_clean: Formative latent variable : why LAVAAN could not compute SE ?
messages.body_plain:
Herve--
     This takes a bit of explaining, but I will try to be brief.  At its core, statistical identification is an algebra problem.  Covariance structure models, from regression on up, imply a structure for the covariance matrix of the observed variables.  The covariance matrix is expressed as a function of model parameters--some with fixed values and some with values that need to be estimated.  Each element of the observed variable covariance matrix is expressed as a function of model parameters.  The algebra problem amounts to finding unique solutions for the unknown parameter values in terms of the knowns--the values of the empirical covariance matrix.  If you can solve uniquely for the unknowns in terms of the knowns, then the solution is identified.
     Some parameters appear in the equations for many elements of the covariance matrix, while some appear in few.  You must solve for each parameter based on those covariance matrix elements where that parameter appears.  If you use up all of those elements solving for other parameters, so that you have nothing left to use in solving for a particular parameter, then identification fails.  (It can fail for other reasons, too.)
     Out of all the unknown parameter values, think just about variances or residual variances.  For observed variables, each diagonal element of the covariance matrix corresponds to the variance of an observed variable, so we can usually solve for those observed variable variance / residual variance parameters out of those diagonal elements.  But for common factors, there are no such "knowns," and we have to look more carefully for places where those variance / residual variance parameters appear.
     Now, whenever we have a regression of a dependent D on a predictor P, we find a regression coefficient, and the core of the formula for a regression coefficient is:

covariance (D, P) / variance (P)

So if your LAT2 were a predictor of some observed variable, we could expect to find the variance / residual variance parameter for LAT2 in the equation for elements of the covariance matrix corresponding to those dependent observed variables.  But no observed variables are dependent on LAT2.  It is also possible that we could find this parameter if other factors were dependent on LAT2.  But that is also not the case here.
     Notice that, if LAT2 is only dependent itself, then its variance / residual variance parameter NEVER appears as a parameter in the equation for any element of the covariance matrix, because we don't need that parameter to compute the regression coefficients (again, see the formula).  That is why LAT2 needs variables dependent on it.
     If you force standardization and fix a path from X1 to LAT2 to 1.0, you are equating X1 and LAT2.  Then you have X1, an observed variable, substituting for the factor LAT2.  Of course, the problem goes away, because the factor LAT2 has gone away, replaced by an observed variable with an element of the covariance matrix corresponding to its total variance.  You get results, but do they mean anything?

--Ed Rigdon

Several notes:

1) the error message "formal argument "SB.classic" matched by multiple
actual arguments.", is a bug in lavaan 0.5-16 (and already fixed in the
dev version); the work around is to call lavTestLRT() directly, with the
SB.classic=FALSE option

2) the SB.classic=FALSE option switches to the 'original' approach to
compute a scaled difference test, as described in Satorra (2000) (see
?lavTestLRT for the full reference). This will always lead to a positive
chi-square test statistic

3) "However the difference test is using the unscaled chi squares rather
than the SB scaled chi-squares.": this is perfectly ok: it is the
difference between the unscaled chi-square statistics that is 'scaled'
in the Satorra (2000) approach, NOT the difference between the scaled
test statistics.

4) The approach using starting values etc (as described in eg
BryantSatorraInPressSEM2011.pdf) is not needed if you are using
SB.classic=FALSE

Yves.

Is there a way to incorporate inequality restrictions on the residual variances, like they can´t exceed observed variances, as to fix the estimation process to a subset and by this trying to avoid my problem in the estimation (maybe this helps!)?

Thanks a lot in advance
Michael

messages.body_plain:
> imputed2<-read.csv("imputed2.csv",header=FALSE)
>
> names(imputed2) <-c("imp", "grade1","gender1","cvict1","cvict2","cvict3","cbul1","cbul2","clim1","clim2","clim3","clim4","teachdo1","peerdo1","agg1", "agg2", "assert1", "assert2","talk1","telladult1", "telladult2","donothing1", "donothing2")
>
> out3 <- runMI(mod2, data=imputed2, chi="all", group="imp", fun="sem", m = 2, std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE)

Here's your problem.  You are passing a single data.frame to runMI(), in which all the imputed copies of your data set are stacked on top of each other, with an indicator "imp" for which imputation it is.  When you call runMI(..., data = <a single data.frame>), the expectation is that you want runMI() to do the imputation step for you (thus, the error message saying it doesn't see any missing values to impute).  If you have already imputed the data, you need to call runMI(..., data = <a list of data.frame objects>), like you did in your simulation.  To see what I mean by a list of data.frames, look at the imputed data sets from Amelia you create in your simulation:

summary(datsimMI$imputations)
lapply(datsimMI$imputations, head)

To take your stacked imputations and put them in a list of individual data.frames, run this code:

my.MI.list <- list()
for (i in as.numeric(names(table(imputed2$imp)))) {
    my.MI.list[[i]] <- imputed2[ imputed2$imp == i , ]
}
lapply(my.MI.list, head)

Then you can pass that list to runMI(... data = my.MI.list) like you do in your simulation.

> t3 <- runMI(mod2, data=test.dat, chi="all",  miPackage="mice",group=".imp", fun="sem", m = 2)
>
> This gives me output for 3 datasets, including the one I have coded as 0 because it is unimputed, when I only want the program to pay attention to the already imputed datasets.

I'm not sure what your "mice3" data looks like, but if you only want runMI() to pay attention to the imputed data sets, then don't include the original (unimputed) data set in the list of data.frames that you pass to runMI().

Terry

messages.subject_clean: Variance of predict()ed factor scores inferior to model estimates?
messages.body_plain:
JB—

     The reason is that what factor software calls “factor scores” are not true factors scores at all.  Factors are typically indeterminate, meaning that they include a component that does not have one specific value.  With true factor scores, this component will be weighted so that it accounts for a share of variance equal to 1 – R2(F, Y), or 1 – the R2 where the observed variables are used to predict the common factor.  The pseudo factor scores produced by factor software omit this component, so you should expect these pseudo factor scores to have variance equal to (1 – R2(F, Y))% of the variance of the factor in your model.  There are other differences, as well.

     If you want to use a factor model but avoid indeterminacy, you need more and better observed variables per factor.  If you want genuine factor scores, it is easy to fabricate the missing component, but remember this component is a vector with no one best set of values, so any particular draw is just one of an infinity of possibilities.  I can refer you to the literature, if you would like to read up.

--Ed Rigdon

Diana--
     If a common factor has 2 indicators, you do not need to constrain the Loadings to equality in order to achieve identification, as long as the factor covaries significantly with something else, like another common factor.  Unless those loading equality constraints for the factors with two indicators are based on prior knowledge, I would remove them.  Understand otherwise that the CFA function is imposing constraints of its own to achieve identification.  It is quite likely that those defaults along would achieve identification for you, without the steps you have taken in this syntax.  On the other hand, I am entirely in favor of specifying your own model, rather than relying on automatic constraints that may not be entirely clear.
--Ed Rigdon

messages.body_plain:
I want to fit a CFA with one latent variable and three categorical indicators. This model is just-identified (DF=0). My indicators have 5 categories and are not normally distributed, so I should use DWLS estimator. My sample needs to be weighted, so I use the lavaan.survey package and include weights.

First of all, I tried fitting this model with lavaan command, like was done in the tutorial " package'lavaan.survey' ", but I got an error message, indicating that something might be going wrong.

Second, I tried fitting this model using sem command. Here I had to error message, but the model was estimated using MLM instead of DWLS.

Any suggestions of an alternative code that would work?
Here is my code and output.

> f <- "C:/.../mydata.csv"
> t <- read.csv(f,sep=";")
>
> u<-t[!is.na <http://is.na>(t$wreg),]
>
> is.numeric(u$q96_1)
[1] TRUE
> is.numeric(u$q96_2)
[1] TRUE
> is.numeric(u$q96_3)
[1] TRUE
> u <- subset(u, q96_1==1| q96_1==2| q96_1==3| q96_1==4| q96_1==5)
> u <- subset(u, q96_2==1| q96_2==2| q96_2==3| q96_2==4| q96_2==5)
> u <- subset(u, q96_3==1| q96_3==2| q96_3==3| q96_3==4| q96_3==5)
> fl <- subset(u, region==1)
> model <- 'ethic =~ q96_1 + q96_2 + q96_3'

# fit using lavaan # error message #
> fit <- lavaan(model, data=fl,ordered=c("q96_1","q96_2","q96_3"))
Erreur dans t(Delta[[g]]) %*% lav...@WLS.V[[g]] :
  arguments inadéquats
De plus : Messages d'avis :
1: In WLS.obs - WLS.est :
  la taille d'un objet plus long n'est pas multiple de la taille d'un objet plus court
2: In lavsamp...@WLS.obs[[g]] - WLS.est[[g]] :
  la taille d'un objet plus long n'est pas multiple de la taille d'un objet plus court

> fit <- sem(model, data=fl,ordered=c("q96_1","q96_2","q96_3"))
> des <- svydesign(ids=~1, data=fl, weights=~wreg)
> fit.survey <- lavaan.survey(fit, des,)
